title: From accepted create to a saved order
scenario: An external ABAP program creates a non-draft managed Order with Comment = Draft, then changes Comment to Ready. It owns the transaction. Follow one successful save, then compare a rejected save.
goal: Distinguish request acceptance, transactional reads and actual persistence.

steps.title: Create is accepted
steps.explanation: MODIFY requests one order. Managed numbering gives it UUID U1 and MAPPED correlates that identity with the request %cid. Inspect FAILED and REPORTED.
steps.outcome: A generated UUID does not prove that a database row is committed.

steps.title: Update and read the same buffer
steps.explanation: Update Comment to Ready. An EML read in the same transaction can return Ready before saving. Handle read/update failures rather than assuming all keys succeeded.
steps.outcome: The transactional result can differ from database state.

steps.title: Ask RAP to save
steps.explanation: The external owner calls COMMIT ENTITIES. RAP runs the applicable save checks and persistence processing. Capture the save status and its separate FAILED/REPORTED response.
steps.outcome: Do not announce success before the save result is known.

steps.title: Successful save
steps.explanation: In the success path, the database now contains U1 with Ready. A later transaction can read the persisted order.
steps.outcome: This is the point where this example can report that the order was saved.

steps.title: Compare: a rejected save
steps.explanation: Start again with no saved order. Suppose an on-save business validation rejects the new order. Retain the failure messages and roll back the pending transaction. No successful create has been committed.
steps.outcome: Do not confuse rollback with deleting an order that was already committed in the success path.

takeaway: Accepted by MODIFY means pending. Saved means the separate save completed successfully.
limitation: A conceptual single-entity example, not an executed SAP transaction. UUID U1 is a readable label. Service consumers let the framework own commit/rollback; behavior handlers must not issue them.

references.title: SAP Learning: EML and transaction ownership
